limitations: Type erasure means unsound casts/any bypass static diagnostics entirely, producing later, less specific runtime errors instead of caught compile-time errors.
Some diagnostic messages for deeply nested generic/conditional types become verbose and hard to parse (structural type mismatch dumps).
No built-in exhaustiveness-checking diagnostic beyond manual never assertions in switch statements.
metric.diagnostics.method: Assessed compile-time and runtime diagnostic quality using tsc static analysis expectations on representative micro/adversarial programs, plus known TypeScript/Node.js runtime error reporting characteristics (stack traces, source maps).
observations: tsc provides structured diagnostics (error code, message, file:line:col, and often a source excerpt) for the type errors intentionally probed by adversarial fixtures such as ADV-01_C.ts/ADV-22 bigint-narrowing conversions.

Deeply recursive adversarial cases (ADV-21_depth1000.ts, ADV-21_depth10000.ts) are designed to trigger runtime RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded, which Node.js reports with a truncated but instrumented stack trace; source maps map back to original .ts lines when enabled.

Because TypeScript type errors are compile-time-only (erased at runtime), certain type violations occurring only through any/unsafe casts or external JS interop surface as opaque runtime TypeErrors rather than the richer compile-time diagnostics.
metric.diagnostics.score_rationale: 80/100: strong, actionable compiler diagnostics with codes and locations, and reasonable runtime stack traces, but erasure-driven unsoundness and occasionally noisy generic-type error messages prevent a higher score.
strengths: tsc diagnostics are precise, include error codes for tooling, and integrate with editors for inline error markers/quick fixes.
Strict-mode flags (strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, etc.) meaningfully raise the floor of static diagnostics.
Runtime stack traces (V8) are informative for uncaught exceptions and include function names/line numbers via source maps.

limitations: No native pattern matching / exhaustive match expression (must emulate via switch + never-check).
No true nominal typing or built-in immutable value types; numeric model still bifurcated between number and bigint (evidenced by ADV-01_C.ts, ADV-22a/b conversions).
Erased generics at runtime (type information not available for runtime reflection) unlike languages with reified generics.
metric.functionality_expressiveness.method: Inspected TypeScript adversarial and micro program corpora under template/programs/typescript/{adversarial,micro} to assess expressive surface: structural typing, union/intersection types, generics, mapped/conditional types, template literal types, discriminated unions, async/await, optional chaining, bigint, typed arrays.
observations: ADV-01_C.ts exercises bigint to Number to Int32Array numeric-conversion narrowing semantics, showing rich builtin numeric type support and typed-array interop.
ADV-22a/ADV-22b probe bigint literal typing and truncation behavior at compile boundaries.

Micro benchmark suite (mb00-mb11) escalates in complexity (22 bytes to about 5KB) covering common algorithmic idioms (loops, arrays, recursion, closures) implementable concisely due to first-class functions, arrow syntax, destructuring, and structural interfaces.

Adversarial suite ADV-11..ADV-26 covers deep recursion (ADV-21 variants up to depth 10000), showing stack-limit behavior and large-input handling that stresses expressive constructs like recursion vs iteration equivalence.
metric.functionality_expressiveness.score_rationale: 88/100: very high expressiveness due to advanced structural/type-level features and modern ergonomic syntax, docked modestly for absence of native pattern matching, reified generics, and the split numeric model exercised by the adversarial suite.
strengths: Structural typing, union/discriminated-union types, generics with variance inference, mapped/conditional/template-literal types give very high type-level expressiveness relative to most mainstream languages.
First-class functions/closures, async/await, optional chaining/nullish coalescing, destructuring, spread, and iterators/generators cover a broad expressiveness surface with concise syntax.
Structural (duck) typing plus algebraic-like discriminated unions approximate sum types without native pattern matching.
